title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Garden maintenance and clean-ups
audience: Garden maintenance and clean-up operators, solo or with a team, who want more recurring work from clients that suit their service, their area and their job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a garden need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. Write down the garden jobs you do well (clean-ups, bed clearing, seasonal upkeep), the price range you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs the work. A monthly upkeep plan on a route you already run is worth far more to a small business than a single large clean-up across town. Vendor market ranges can test a prospect's budget: Airtasker lists monthly upkeep at $120 to $220 and a one-off clean-up at $200 to $600 or more (Airtasker, 18 June 2026). Those are marketplace ranges, not a regulator's figures.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria: inside your service area, a repeat need, a reachable decision-maker, and a job that your insurance covers. Strata committees appoint contractors, and their growing-season tasks include routine garden work (Clean Group, 9 March 2026), so a strata manager with several gardens in your area can be a strong fit. Councils buy routine gardening and clean-up for council buildings and parks on a schedule of rates (Central Coast Council, Tasmania, tender closing 10 November 2025), so councils are a segment to research in your own state. Housing providers also tender cyclical garden maintenance (CHVL tender, Victoria, closing 14 September 2025). Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Write one short profile for each segment, as business.gov.au suggests (24 September 2024). Keep only business contact details published for business use, and do not use bought or harvested lists (ACMA, Spam Act obligations, last updated 28 March 2019).

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely soon. For garden work the useful signals are public tenders and forward plans. In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders, lets suppliers set alerts, and publishes each agency's annual plan of what it intends to buy (Buying for Victoria, 7 August 2026). Each state runs its own portal, and national tender listings help you spot councils in other states. Council planning registers show projects at application stage, such as the City of Casey register in Victoria's open-data portal (DataVic, updated 5 November 2026). Use signals to decide when to contact an organisation, not to build a profile of individuals. Do not approach a household about its garden because you saw a public record about the address.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message states how you learned about the need, makes one observation you can verify from public view or from the organisation's own published material (for example, a tender schedule for seasonal clean-ups that you can meet), and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined area or a fifteen-minute call. Keep it short and do not overstate what you know. Where the message goes by email or text, check the consent and unsubscribe rules first. The ACCC's July 2026 review found that many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading and that many salespeople did not identify themselves, so a specific, honest message that names you is a practical advantage as well as a compliance step (ACCC, 28 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be, and write the plan down before the first message. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work, and move your effort toward them. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the job, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the garden work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, such as tender alerts, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the licence rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A small garden business covers three suburbs in Victoria. A housing provider's tender for cyclical garden maintenance on properties in one suburb is listed, and the business can meet the monthly schedule and the photographic evidence rule.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner respond to the tender, and what should the response contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner checks the tender's scope, schedule and evidence rules against what the business can deliver, and confirms that its insurance meets the tender terms. The response goes through the route the tender sets. If the owner also wants to email a named contact, the owner checks the Spam Act first: ACMA says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The owner does not contact tenants or residents with personal details, and does not enter the properties uninvited. The response states the scope the business can deliver, the monthly schedule, the evidence it will provide and one question about access.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. No licence rule for routine gardening was found in the sources read; this is not confirmed for other states. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. ACMA's avoid-spam guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7) says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Whether the Act applies to a small business is not confirmed in this lesson.

Telemarketing calls to registered numbers are limited to weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm, and never on Sundays or public holidays (Do Not Call Register industry guide, 2018 copyright notice; check for updates). Wash any call list against the register before calling.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the garden work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, such as tenders, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public tender for cyclical garden maintenance is listed in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Respond through the tender's own route, after checking that you can meet its scope, schedule and evidence rules
Message each resident using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the work
Go onto the site to look at the gardens and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending
